items.stem: A rational consumer should continue to buy more units of a good as long as
options: the marginal benefit is at least equal to the marginal cost
items.answer: the marginal benefit is at least equal to the marginal cost
items.markingKey: Buy while MB ≥ MC; stop where MB = MC.

items.stem: Which is the main reason a government might provide a good itself?
options: The good is very cheap to produce
The market would not provide it because of the free rider problem
items.answer: The market would not provide it because of the free rider problem
items.markingKey: Public goods.

items.stem: Fenwick & Co reorganises its laptops factory in Riyadh so that each worker does a single task. Explain one benefit and one drawback for Fenwick & Co.
items.answer: Benefit: higher productivity, lower unit costs. Drawback: boredom and lower motivation, higher absence/labour turnover, or disruption if one stage stops.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefit; 1 mark: drawback [3]

items.stem: The government of Kestria uses tariffs because it has difficulty collecting income tax. Which argument for protection is being used?
items.answer: Raising government revenue
items.markingKey: Raising government revenue: tariffs are easy to collect at the border.

items.stem: An airline cuts fares on the route from Mumbai to a holiday island and sales rise sharply. Explain why demand may be price elastic.
items.answer: Holiday flights are a luxury with many substitutes (other airlines, destinations) and take a large share of income, so demand responds strongly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies elastic; 1 mark: reason [3]

items.stem: In Istrana, a rise in the price of cinema tickets quickly attracts new private firms into the industry with no government involvement. Which type of economic system does this describe?
items.answer: Market economy
items.markingKey: Market economy: price signals and the profit motive guide resource allocation.

items.stem: What is meant by trade creation?
options: The creation of a new trading bloc
An increase in tariffs on non-members
A shift from higher-cost domestic production to lower-cost imports from a bloc partner
A shift from low-cost non-member imports to higher-cost member imports
items.answer: A shift from higher-cost domestic production to lower-cost imports from a bloc partner
items.markingKey: Efficiency gain from joining a bloc.

items.stem: Which function of price provides information to producers and consumers about market conditions?
items.answer: Signalling
items.markingKey: Price changes are signals.

items.stem: In a revision note Omar wrote: ‘The AD curve slopes downwards for the same reason as a demand curve for a single good.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A single good’s demand curve relies on substitution between goods; the AD curve reflects wealth, interest rate and international trade effects of a change in the general price level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A single good’s demand curve relies on substitution between goods; the AD curve reflects wealth, interest rate and international trade effects of a change in the general price level. [3]

items.stem: The table shows a simplified consumer price index for Merania. Category: Energy, Food, Transport; Weight: 45, 35, 20; Price change (%): 5, 3, 10. Calculate the rate of inflation.
In a revision note Daniel wrote: ‘The central bank of Nordavia collects taxes and decides government spending.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Taxes and spending are fiscal policy decided by the government; the central bank conducts monetary policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Taxes and spending are fiscal policy decided by the government; the central bank conducts monetary policy. [3]

items.stem: Unemployment in Pelora (thousands): frictional 250, structural 500, cyclical 600, seasonal 50. The labour force is 20 million. Calculate the unemployment rate.
Elena wrote in a homework answer: ‘Means-tested benefits are always better because they only go to the poor.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: They cost less, but take-up is often low, they are costly to administer and can create a poverty trap.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – They cost less, but take-up is often low, they are costly to administer and can create a poverty trap. [3]

items.stem: Sundara: Year: 1, 2, 3, 4; Real GDP ($ billion): 500, 505, 530.2, 540.8. Calculate the growth rate of real GDP in Year 3.
A student, Lucas, claims: ‘A current account deficit always means that Lunaria is poorer.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable. [2]

items.stem: In the market for printed newspapers, Qd = 98 − 4P and Qs = 26 + 2P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government introduces a maximum price of $9. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity without intervention. (b) Calculate quantity demanded and supplied at the controlled price and the resulting shortage. (c) Explain one way in which the shortage may be allocated and one likely consequence.
items.answer: (a) $12, 50 thousand. (b) Qd = 62, Qs = 44: shortage of 18 thousand. (c) Queuing, waiting lists or rationing; black market at higher prices.

items.stem: Valdoria spends $8bn on a training programme for 250,000 workers. Each trained worker’s output rises by $4,000 a year for 10 years. Calculate the total extra output over the period (ignoring discounting).
items.answer: $10bn

items.stem: A sudden heatwave raises demand for fans in Sundara. Explain why Silverline, which holds large stocks, could benefit more than its rivals.
items.answer: Stocks make its supply elastic: it can increase sales quickly while rivals cannot, gaining revenue and market share.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: elastic supply; 1 mark: benefit [2]

items.stem: In Ostrelia, government spending is $180bn, tax revenue is $190bn and GDP is $1000bn. The national debt at the start of the year is $600bn. Calculate the budget balance as a percentage of GDP.
Istrana moves resources from producing washing machines to producing smartphones. Using a PPC, explain why the opportunity cost of extra smartphones rises as more is produced.
items.answer: Workers and machines best suited to smartphones move first; later the resources moved are less suited, so more washing machines must be given up for each extra unit of smartphones: a concave PPC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources not equally suited; 1 mark: rising sacrifice/concave PPC [2]

items.stem: Firms in Lunaria invest heavily in factories abroad. What is the most likely effect on the market for the currency of Lunaria? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates: outward investment requires selling the currency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates; 1 mark: explanation – outward investment requires selling the currency. [2]

items.stem: Classify each policy as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and explain how it could reduce a current account deficit. (i) The government of Quentara funds training to raise productivity in export industries. (ii) Quentara subsidises its exporters of bottled water.
items.answer: (i) Supply-side policy: improves competitiveness in the long run. (ii) Expenditure-switching policy: lowers export prices so foreign spending switches to Quentara’s goods.
items.markingKey: (i) Supply-side policy [1]; explanation [1] (ii) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $2.0 to $2.6 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Pelora, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Seoul still rose slightly because incomes grew by 5% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain the effect of the frosts on the supply curve of coffee beans. (c) Explain why sales of tea fell.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. (c) Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.6 − 2.0)/2.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. [2] (c) Credit: Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. [2]

items.stem: In Rovania, nominal GDP rose from $600 billion in the base year to $648 billion a year later. The GDP deflator rose from 100 to 105. Population rose from 8 million to 8.2 million. (a) Calculate real GDP and the real growth rate. (b) Calculate real GDP per capita in each year and its percentage change. (c) Comment on what has happened to average living standards.
items.answer: (a) Real GDP $617.1bn; growth +2.9%. (b) $75,000 → $75,261.32; +0.3%. (c) Average material living standards rose, though GDP per capita ignores distribution and non-market factors.
items.markingKey: (a) deflate [1]; growth [1] (b) per capita values [1]; change [1] (c) comment with limitation [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Rovania has $600 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($150 million), a rail link to Kathmandu ($200 million) and a programme of school building ($350 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much more than the budget would be needed to fund all three projects. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (c) Discuss how the government should decide which project to fund.
items.answer: (a) $100 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (c) Compare benefits and opportunity costs; consider who gains (for whom), long-run effects on growth, equity and public opinion; data may be uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 150 + 200 + 350 = 700; |700 − 600| = 100 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (c) 2 marks: analysis of criteria; 2 marks: evaluation and conclusion [4]

items.stem: Extract: The market for restaurant meals in Lagos is described by Qd = 84 − 3P and Qs = 28 + 4P (Q in thousands per month, P in dollars). The city council is considering a tax on restaurant meals, which some councillors say would “simply transfer money from consumers to the council”. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Calculate consumer surplus at equilibrium. (c) Calculate producer surplus at equilibrium. (d) Explain how a tax would affect consumer and producer surplus.
items.answer: (a) $8, 60 (b) $600,000 (c) $352,000 (d) Price to consumers rises and price received by producers falls; both surpluses fall; part becomes tax revenue, part is a deadweight loss.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $8, 60 [2] (b) ½ × (28 − 8) × 60 [2] (c) Credit: $352,000 [2] (d) Credit: Price to consumers rises and price received by producers falls; both surpluses fall; part becomes tax revenue, part is a deadweight loss. [3]

items.stem: Data for Halvoria: Item ($ billion): Investment, Saving, Government spending, Taxation, Exports, Imports; Value: 100, 130, 200, 180, 150, 110. (a) Calculate total injections and total leakages. (b) Explain what will happen to national income.
items.answer: (a) Injections $450bn; leakages $420bn. (b) National income will rise: more is added to the flow than withdrawn, so output and income rise until leakages equal injections.
items.markingKey: (a) both totals [2] (b) direction [1]; explanation [1] [4]

items.stem: Newspapers in Jovania have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. Explain the main macroeconomic objectives of a government.
items.answer: Sustainable growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation, BoP stability; why each matters; how measured.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Sustainable growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation, BoP stability; why each matters; how measured. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Classify each good and explain your answer. (i) Sugary fizzy drinks sold to teenagers in Lima. (ii) A lighthouse warning ships off the coast of Tarvia.
items.answer: (i) Demerit good (ii) Public good
items.markingKey: (i) Demerit good – the harm to health is underestimated by consumers. [2] (ii) Public good – non-excludable and non-rivalrous; free riders cannot be prevented. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: In Selmaria the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 20 to 25 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 400 million to 380 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Identify one positive and one normative statement in the minister’s comment. (c) Explain how the government could use marginal analysis to decide the size of the tax. (d) Discuss whether the effects of the tax are likely to be greater in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 5% (b) “Sugar taxes work” (reduce consumption) is positive/testable; “every country should have one” is normative. (c) Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). (d) In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) (400 − 380)/400 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) Credit: Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). [2] (d) Credit: In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement. [4]

items.stem: The government of Esteria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain how information failure can cause markets to fail.
items.answer: Imperfect and asymmetric information; merit/demerit goods; second-hand markets; insurance; consumers misjudge benefits and costs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Imperfect and asymmetric information; merit/demerit goods; second-hand markets; insurance; consumers misjudge benefits and costs. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Newspapers in Valdoria have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. Explain the role of the entrepreneur in a market economy.
items.answer: Organises land, labour and capital; takes decisions; bears uninsurable risk; innovates; rewarded by profit; signals from prices.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Organises land, labour and capital; takes decisions; bears uninsurable risk; innovates; rewarded by profit; signals from prices. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: In Rovania, the domestic demand for cement is Qd = 151 − 6P and domestic supply is Qs = −5 + 3P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units a year. Rovania can import any quantity at the world price of $12. The government imposes a tariff of $2 per unit. (a) Calculate domestic production and imports before and after the tariff. (b) Calculate the government’s tariff revenue.
items.answer: (a) Before: P = $12, Qd = 79, Qs = 31, imports = 48 thousand. After: P = $14, Qd = 67, Qs = 37, imports = 30 thousand. (b) 2 × 30 thousand = $60,000.
items.markingKey: (a) before [1]; after [2] (b) revenue [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Research for the government of Dravonia estimates that the PED for petrol is −0.4, the YED for air travel is +1.5 and the XED between bus travel and the price of petrol is +0.8. The government plans a tax that would raise the price of petrol by 15%. Incomes are forecast to grow by 3% next year. (a) Calculate the expected percentage change in demand for bus travel. (b) Discuss whether the petrol tax will achieve both a large rise in tax revenue and a large fall in pollution.
items.answer: (a) +12% (b) Inelastic demand → revenue rises but consumption falls little; conflict between objectives; long-run PED higher (electric cars, buses with XED > 0); estimates uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.8 × 15 [1] (b) Credit: Inelastic demand → revenue rises but consumption falls little; conflict between objectives; long-run PED higher (electric cars, buses with XED > 0); estimates uncertain; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Planners in Sundara set the price of washing machines below the market level. At this price 520 thousand households want to buy washing machines each year, but the plan provides only 400 thousand. (a) Calculate the shortage. (b) Explain two ways in which the shortage might be dealt with, and one likely consequence.
items.answer: (a) 120 thousand units. (b) Queuing (first come, first served), waiting lists, rationing by allocation or vouchers, priority by need; consequence: black markets selling at higher prices, or time wasted queuing.
items.markingKey: (a) 520 − 400 = 120 [1] (b) two allocation methods [2]; consequence [1] [4]

items.stem: What is the balance of trade in goods?
options: Exports of services minus imports of services
The value of exports of goods minus the value of imports of goods
items.answer: The value of exports of goods minus the value of imports of goods
items.markingKey: Also called the visible balance.

items.stem: Higher interest rates reduce investment because
options: the cost of borrowing to finance projects rises
items.answer: the cost of borrowing to finance projects rises
items.markingKey: Fewer projects profitable.

items.stem: A student, Noah, claims: ‘A person’s salary is part of their wealth.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A salary is income (a flow); wealth is the stock of assets owned.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A salary is income (a flow); wealth is the stock of assets owned. [2]

items.stem: In Merania: consumption $500bn, investment $120bn, government spending $250bn, exports $200bn and imports $220bn. Calculate aggregate demand.
In a revision note Zara wrote: ‘A depreciation will always improve the current account of Rovania.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: It improves only if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds; in the short run (J-curve) it may worsen the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It improves only if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds; in the short run (J-curve) it may worsen the current account. [2]

items.stem: Mateo runs a business selling rice. In one month Mateo sells 1,000 units at $4 each. Variable costs are $2.4 per unit and fixed costs are $3,000. Mateo gave up a job paying $2,500 a month to run the business. Calculate the monthly accounting profit.
What is the difference between an increase in demand and an increase in quantity demanded?
options: An increase in quantity demanded is caused by a rise in income
An increase in demand is a shift of the curve; an increase in quantity demanded is a movement along it
An increase in demand is caused by a fall in price
items.answer: An increase in demand is a shift of the curve; an increase in quantity demanded is a movement along it
items.markingKey: Terminology: shift vs extension.

items.stem: Which is the best example of a public good?
options: A flood defence system protecting a town
items.answer: A flood defence system protecting a town
items.markingKey: Non-excludable and non-rivalrous within the protected area.

items.stem: Buyers of second-hand cars in Bangkok often cannot tell whether a car has hidden faults. Explain how this asymmetric information affects the market.
items.answer: Sellers know more than buyers; buyers fear buying a “lemon”, so they offer low prices; owners of good cars withdraw, so the market shrinks and average quality falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: asymmetric information; 1 mark: effect on price/quality [2]

items.stem: The government of Westaria funds free vocational training for young workers. What type of supply-side policy is this?
items.answer: Interventionist supply-side policy
items.markingKey: Interventionist supply-side policy: government directly invests in human capital.

items.stem: As incomes in Loristan rose, sales of cheap instant noodles fell while sales of restaurant meals rose strongly. Explain what this shows about the income elasticities of the two goods.
items.answer: Instant noodles: negative YED (inferior). Restaurant meals: positive and probably > 1 (luxury).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Merania privatises its state airline and removes regulations on competition. Which type of policy is this?
items.answer: Supply-side policy
items.markingKey: Supply-side policy: aims to raise efficiency and LRAS.

items.stem: Aisha wrote in a homework answer: ‘The unemployment rate is the number unemployed divided by the whole population.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: The unemployment rate is the number unemployed as a percentage of the labour force (employed + unemployed), not the whole population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The unemployment rate is the number unemployed as a percentage of the labour force (employed + unemployed), not the whole population. [2]

items.stem: In a recession, GDP in Westaria falls by 2% from $500bn. Tax revenue is 40% of GDP, and 100 thousand more people claim unemployment benefit of $10,000 a year each. Calculate the fall in tax revenue.
items.answer: $4bn

items.stem: Ana makes the following statement: ‘In the circular flow, households supply goods and services to firms.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Households supply factors of production; firms supply goods and services to households.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Households supply factors of production; firms supply goods and services to households. [2]

items.stem: Demand for laptops is Qd = 120 − 2P. After a rise in production costs, supply changes from Qs = 0 + 4P to Qs = −12 + 4P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before and after. (b) Calculate consumer surplus before and after. (c) Explain why consumers have gained or lost.
items.answer: (a) $20, 80 → $22, 76. (b) $1,600,000 → $1,444,000. (c) Higher price for remaining buyers and some priced out: CS falls.
items.markingKey: (a) both equilibria [2] (b) both CS values [2] (c) explanation [1] [5]

items.stem: Freya saves $20,000 for a year at a nominal interest rate of 1%. Inflation over the year is 2%. What is the approximate real interest rate?
Many workers from Loristan work abroad and send income home, while foreign firms in Loristan send profits overseas. Explain how this affects the difference between Loristan’s GDP and GNI.
items.answer: Income earned abroad by residents adds to GNI; profits paid to foreign owners are subtracted. GNI exceeds GDP if inflows are larger than outflows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflows add; 1 mark: outflows subtract [2]

items.stem: Istrana spends $40bn a year on imported consumer goods and has a current account deficit of $12bn. It imposes a 15% tariff on these imports. The price elasticity of demand for the imports is −2. Assuming the full tariff is passed on to consumers, calculate the percentage change in the volume of imports.

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the meaning of the question “what to produce?” and why it arises. (b) Explain the different objectives that households, firms and the government are assumed to pursue.
items.answer: (a) It concerns which goods and services, and how much of each, an economy should make with its scarce resources; it arises because resources cannot produce everything wanted. (b) Households aim to maximise utility (satisfaction) from consumption; firms aim to maximise profit; government aims to maximise the welfare of society as a whole.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: which goods and quantities; 1 mark: arises from scarcity [2] (b) 1 mark each agent correctly linked to objective [3]

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of units of output for a council in Pelora. Number of units of output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 60, 48, 40, 24, 20, 10; Marginal cost ($): 25, 35, 41, 49, 65, 65. (a) State the quantity that maximises net benefit and explain why. (b) Calculate the total net benefit at this quantity.
items.answer: (a) 2: every unit up to 2 has MB ≥ MC; the next has MC > MB. (b) $48
items.markingKey: (a) 2 [1]; MB ≥ MC rule [1] (b) Σ(MB − MC) for units 1–2 = 48 [2] Total [4]

items.stem: A tariff on imported televisions in Selmaria raises consumers’ spending on televisions by $120m a year and is estimated to save 3,000 jobs in domestic factories. The average wage in the industry is $22,000 a year. (a) Calculate the cost to consumers of each job saved. (b) Compare this with the average wage and comment.
items.answer: (a) $120m / 3,000 = $40,000. (b) This is 1.8 times the average wage, so it would be cheaper to pay the workers’ wages directly or to fund retraining; protection is a costly way to save jobs.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) comparison [1]; comment [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Sundara rose from 6% to 13%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 25% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Calculate the change in unemployment in percentage points. (b) Discuss whether the investment programme will make the people of Sundara better off.
items.answer: (a) 7 percentage points (b) Outward shift of the PPC in future, more consumer goods later, jobs now (idle resources used: no opportunity cost in a recession) vs lower consumption at full employment, risk of poor projects, debt; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 13 − 6 [1] (b) Credit: Outward shift of the PPC in future, more consumer goods later, jobs now (idle resources used: no opportunity cost in a recession) vs lower consumption at full employment, risk of poor projects, debt; judgement. [5]

items.stem: For each case, identify the likely price elasticity of supply and explain why. (i) Horizon Corp operates its furniture factory at only 60% of capacity. (ii) Only a few highly trained surgeons can perform a new operation in Gorvania.
items.answer: (i) Elastic supply (ii) Inelastic supply
items.markingKey: (i) Elastic supply – spare capacity allows output to rise quickly. [2] (ii) Inelastic supply – specialist skills make labour immobile in the short run. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Ostrelia plans to tax bottled water to reduce consumption. Economists estimate the market as Qd = 60 − 2P and Qs = 10 + 3P (Q in thousands per week, P in dollars). The proposed tax is $2 per unit. Some ministers prefer a ban on advertising or a public information campaign instead. (a) Calculate the new price paid by consumers and the new quantity. (b) Calculate the weekly tax revenue. (c) Discuss whether a tax is better than regulation or information as a way of reducing consumption.
items.answer: (a) $11.20, 37.6 (b) $75,200 (c) Tax: price signal, revenue, but regressive, smuggling, inelastic demand; regulation certain but costly to enforce; information tackles cause but slow; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $11.20, 37.6 [2] (b) 2 × 37.6 thousand [1] (c) Credit: Tax: price signal, revenue, but regressive, smuggling, inelastic demand; regulation certain but costly to enforce; information tackles cause but slow; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Lunaria was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 2.0% to 6.5%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.28 to 0.42, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) State the type of economic system that Lunaria has now. Give a reason. (b) Explain why inequality may have increased. (c) Discuss whether the move to a market economy has been beneficial for the people of Lunaria.
items.answer: (a) Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. (b) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. (c) Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. [2] (b) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2] (c) Credit: Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Real GDP per head in Sundara rose by 40% over ten years, while CO₂ emissions per head rose by 60% and the income share of the richest 10% rose from 30% to 36%. Using the data, explain one benefit and two costs of this growth.
items.answer: Benefit: higher average incomes and consumption (40% rise in real GDP per head). Costs: environmental damage (emissions up 60%, faster than output); rising inequality (top 10% share up 6 percentage points).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefit with data; 1 mark each cost with data [3]

items.stem: Exports account for 45% of the GDP of Selmaria. Explain the benefits of free trade and specialisation for an economy.
items.answer: Higher output through comparative advantage, lower prices and more choice, economies of scale, competition and efficiency, technology transfer.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Higher output through comparative advantage, lower prices and more choice, economies of scale, competition and efficiency, technology transfer. items.stem: In the market for gym memberships, Qd = 98 − 4P and Qs = −10 + 5P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). After a successful advertising campaign, the demand equation becomes Qd = 107 − 4P. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before and after the change. (b) Explain the process by which the market reaches the new equilibrium.
items.answer: (a) Before: P = $12, Q = 50; after: P = $13, Q = 55. (b) Demand shifts right: excess demand at the old price pushes price up; supply extends until a new equilibrium.
items.markingKey: (a) old equilibrium [1]; new equilibrium [2] (b) shift, disequilibrium and adjustment [2] [5]

items.stem: Extract: Umbria Nova’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 210, imports of goods 320, exports of services 95, imports of services 70, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $800bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative. (c) Discuss whether Umbria Nova’s current account position is a serious problem.
items.answer: (a) −$87bn; −10.9% of GDP. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. (c) Size relative to GDP, cyclical vs structural cause, consumption- not investment-led, financing by foreign bond holders (risk of capital flight), possible depreciation; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$87bn; −10.9% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2] (c) Credit: Size relative to GDP, cyclical vs structural cause, consumption- not investment-led, financing by foreign bond holders (risk of capital flight), possible depreciation; judgement. [6]

items.stem: The government of Fendaria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain the instruments of monetary policy, including quantitative easing.
items.answer: Policy rate, open market operations, reserve requirements, QE; how each affects money supply and interest rates.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Policy rate, open market operations, reserve requirements, QE; how each affects money supply and interest rates. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: The government of Umbria Nova has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain the difference between universal and means-tested benefits.
items.answer: Universal: all in group regardless of income; means-tested: targeted by income/wealth; examples; take-up, cost, stigma, poverty trap.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Universal: all in group regardless of income; means-tested: targeted by income/wealth; examples; take-up, cost, stigma, poverty trap.
