items.stem: In Umbria Nova, the labour force grew from 30 million to 31.5 million and output per worker at full employment rose from $25,000 to $26,000. (a) Calculate potential output before and after, and the percentage increase. (b) Explain the effect on the LRAS curve and on the economy’s productive capacity.
items.answer: (a) $750bn → $819bn: +9.2%. (b) LRAS shifts right: more and more productive labour raises full-employment output.
items.markingKey: (a) both values [1]; % change [1] (b) LRAS shift [1]; reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The naira, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 8 naira to $1 = 10 naira over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Loristan has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 7% from 4%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) State whether this is a depreciation or a devaluation, and explain why. (b) Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how the cut in interest rates caused the fall.
items.answer: (a) Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. (b) Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. [2] (b) Credit: Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. [4]

items.stem: At Fenwick & Co, 6 workers each make complete cakes, producing 4 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 60 cakes a day. Each worker is paid $40 a day. (a) Calculate output per worker and the labour cost per unit before and after. (b) Explain why output per worker rose. (c) Explain one possible drawback of the change for Fenwick & Co.
items.answer: (a) Output per worker 4 → 10; labour cost per unit $10 → $4. (b) Workers become quicker and more skilled at one task, no time lost switching tasks, specialist tools. (c) Boredom/low motivation, absenteeism or disruption if one stage stops.
items.markingKey: (a) output per worker both [1]; cost per unit 40/4 and 40/10 [2] (b) reason [1] (c) drawback [1] [5]

items.stem: What is the opportunity cost of moving from a point inside the PPC to a point on the curve with more of both goods?
options: The cost of the resources used
items.answer: Zero
items.markingKey: Idle resources are brought into use; nothing is given up.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) How does better infrastructure increase aggregate supply? (b) Why might the government fund research and development?
items.answer: (a) It reduces firms’ transport and communication costs and raises productivity (b) R&D creates positive externalities that the market under-provides
items.markingKey: (a) LRAS shifts right. (b) Spillovers.

items.stem: Lumen Ltd researches a new vaccine that other firms can copy. Explain why the market may provide too little research.
items.answer: Research creates positive externalities (benefits to other firms and society) that Lumen Ltd cannot charge for, so it invests less than the social optimum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: external benefits; 1 mark: under-investment [3]

items.stem: The yuan appreciates by 18% and exporters of chocolate bars in Loristan lay off workers. Which effect of the exchange rate change is shown?
options: Higher net exports and economic growth
items.answer: Higher unemployment in export industries
items.markingKey: Higher unemployment in export industries: exports become dearer and demand falls.

items.stem: Freya would have paid up to $120 for a concert ticket in Muscat but bought it for $75. Explain what is meant by Freya’s consumer surplus and calculate it.
items.answer: Consumer surplus is the difference between willingness to pay and the price paid: $120 − $75 = $45.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition; 1 mark: $45 [3]

items.stem: Indicator: Real GDP growth (%), Unemployment (%), Inflation (%), Current account (% of GDP); Selmaria: 1.5, 9, 2.2, −7; Istrana: 5, 7, 2, −2. Using targets of growth ≥ 2%, unemployment ≤ 5%, inflation 1–3% and a current account within ±3% of GDP, which country meets more objectives?
items.answer: Istrana
items.markingKey: Selmaria meets 1, Istrana meets 3.

items.stem: Why is consumption of domestic output not an injection?
options: It is part of the existing circular flow of income
It is not counted in GDP
items.answer: It is part of the existing circular flow of income
items.markingKey: Induced spending from income.

items.stem: Why is PED usually negative?
options: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
items.answer: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
items.markingKey: Law of demand.

items.stem: In a revision note Chloe wrote: ‘Free trade benefits every worker in Jovania.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers. [3]

items.stem: A government bond in Rovania pays a fixed $50 a year. After central bank purchases (quantitative easing), its market price rises from $800 to $880. Calculate the new yield on the bond.
Nordavia has grown at 8% a year for a decade, but air pollution in Madrid has worsened. Explain why growth may not have improved welfare as much as GDP suggests.
items.answer: Pollution harms health and quality of life, a cost not measured in GDP; gains may also be unequally shared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: externality not in GDP; 1 mark: welfare effect [3]

items.stem: In Merania, average wages rose by 8% while labour productivity rose by 1%. Calculate the approximate change in unit labour costs.
In a revision note Ethan wrote: ‘A tariff makes everyone in Calvania better off because domestic firms sell more.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Producers and the government gain, but consumers lose more than they gain, so there is a net deadweight loss; exporters may lose through retaliation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Producers and the government gain, but consumers lose more than they gain, so there is a net deadweight loss; exporters may lose through retaliation. [3]

items.stem: Amara, who designs and launches a new app and takes the financial risk. Which factor of production is this?
items.answer: Enterprise
items.markingKey: Enterprise: innovation and risk-bearing; earns profit.

items.stem: A drought raises food prices and the cost of agricultural inputs in Merania. Explain the effect on SRAS.
items.answer: Costs of production rise for firms using these inputs, so they supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher costs; 1 mark: SRAS left [2]

items.stem: Esteria cuts government spending to reduce its deficit, and economic growth falls to 0.5%. Which outcome does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Conflict between the current account and economic growth: lower AD reduces real output growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Conflict between the current account and economic growth; 1 mark: explanation – lower AD reduces real output growth. [2]

items.stem: An economist studies the effect of a rise in the price of concert tickets on sales, holding incomes, tastes and other prices constant. Which aspect of economic method does this illustrate?
items.answer: Ceteris paribus assumption
items.markingKey: Ceteris paribus assumption: only one variable is changed while others are held equal.

items.stem: A student, Lina, claims: ‘Equity means that everyone should have exactly the same income.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Equity means fairness; equality means the same shares. A fair distribution may still be unequal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Equity means fairness; equality means the same shares. A fair distribution may still be unequal. [2]

items.stem: Demand for tomatoes increases so that, at the original price, buyers want 40% more. The PES is 0.5 and the PED is −0.5. Which is the most likely outcome?
options: Price rises by about 40% and quantity by about 0%
Price rises by about 20% and quantity by about 40%
Price rises by about 80% and quantity by about 10%
Price rises by about 40% and quantity by about 20%
items.answer: Price rises by about 40% and quantity by about 20%

items.stem: In a revision note Jonas wrote: ‘A subsidy to producers shifts the supply curve to the left because the government pays part of the price.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A subsidy lowers producers’ costs, so supply increases: the curve shifts to the right.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A subsidy lowers producers’ costs, so supply increases: the curve shifts to the right. [2]

items.stem: In the market for concert tickets, Qd = 58 − 3P and Qs = 4 + 6P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government imposes a specific tax of $3 per unit. (a) Calculate the equilibrium before the tax and the new price paid by consumers, price received by producers and quantity. (b) Calculate the tax revenue and the share of the tax paid by consumers. (c) Explain why consumers bear this share.
items.answer: (a) Before: $6, 40. After: consumers pay $8, producers receive $5, Q = 34. (b) Revenue = 3 × 34 thousand = $102,000; consumers bear 67% (consumer burden $68,000, producer burden $34,000). (c) Demand is less elastic than supply (b < d in slope terms), so most of the tax is passed on.
items.markingKey: (a) original equilibrium [1]; new prices and quantity [2] (b) revenue [1]; consumer share 2/3 [1] (c) relative elasticities [1] [6]

items.stem: A farmer in Calvania can use a field to grow either 360 bales of cotton or 60 tonnes of maize in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one tonne of maize in terms of cotton. (b) Calculate how much cotton is given up if the farmer grows 20 tonnes of maize. (c) Explain why the opportunity cost may not stay constant if the farmer uses more fields of differing quality.
items.answer: (a) 6 bales of cotton (b) 120 bales (c) Land is not equally suited to both crops; as more land switches, less suitable land is used, so more cotton must be given up per extra unit of maize (increasing opportunity cost).
items.markingKey: (a) 360/60 [1] (b) 20 × 6 = 120 [1] (c) resources not equally suited [1]; increasing opportunity cost [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Tarvia’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 240, imports of goods 290, exports of services 95, imports of services 70, primary income balance −8, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $800bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain two possible causes of the deficit on trade in goods.
items.answer: (a) −$23bn; −2.9% of GDP. (b) Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$23bn; −2.9% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. [4]

items.stem: Classify each and explain. (i) Tax revenue in Esteria falls automatically as incomes fall in a recession. (ii) The government of Esteria announces a new $20bn road-building programme to fight a recession.
items.answer: (i) Automatic stabiliser (ii) Discretionary fiscal policy
items.markingKey: (i) Automatic stabiliser – revenue changes with the cycle without a policy decision. [2] (ii) Discretionary fiscal policy – a deliberate policy decision. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Pelora was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 2.0% to 6.5%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.28 to 0.42, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) Explain why growth may have increased after the reforms. (b) Discuss whether the move to a market economy has been beneficial for the people of Pelora.
items.answer: (a) Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. (b) Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. [3] (b) Credit: Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Extract: The market for bus journeys in Kestria can be represented by Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 0 + 6P (Q in thousands per month, P in dollars). A popular social media campaign has increased demand by 9 thousand units at every price. Producers say they cannot increase output quickly because of a shortage of skilled workers. (a) Calculate the original equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Calculate the excess demand at the original price after the campaign. (c) Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity. (d) Discuss whether the shortage of skilled workers means the price rise will be large and long-lasting.
items.answer: (a) P = $10, Q = 60 (b) 9 thousand (c) P = $11, Q = 66 (d) Inelastic supply → large price rise in short run; in long run training, migration, technology and entry raise supply; campaign may be a fad; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Solve 90 − 3P = 0 + 6P [2] (b) New Qd at 10 = 69; Qs = 60 [1] (c) 99 − 3P = 0 + 6P [2] (d) Credit: Inelastic supply → large price rise in short run; in long run training, migration, technology and entry raise supply; campaign may be a fad; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Street lighting in Muscat. How is this good best classified? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Public good: non-excludable and non-rivalrous.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Public good; 1 mark: explanation – non-excludable and non-rivalrous. [2]

items.stem: Newspapers in Korvia have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. Explain the three methods of measuring national income and why they should give the same result.
items.answer: Output (value added), income (factor incomes), expenditure (C + I + G + X − M); circular flow identity; exclude transfers and second-hand sales; GDP, GNI, NNI.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Output (value added), income (factor incomes), expenditure (C + I + G + X − M); circular flow identity; exclude transfers and second-hand sales; GDP, GNI, NNI. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Unemployment in Calvania (thousands): frictional 300, structural 600, cyclical 300, seasonal 50. The labour force is 25 million. (a) Calculate the unemployment rate and the share of unemployment that is cyclical. (b) Calculate the unemployment rate if expansionary policy removed all cyclical unemployment. (c) Explain why demand-side policy cannot remove the rest.
items.answer: (a) 5%; cyclical 24% of the unemployed. (b) 3.8% (c) Frictional, structural and seasonal unemployment are not caused by lack of demand; they need supply-side measures (information, retraining, mobility).
items.markingKey: (a) rate [1]; share [1] (b) [1] (c) explanation [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Quentara rose from 4% to 9%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 15% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Calculate the change in unemployment in percentage points. (b) Explain the opportunity cost of the investment programme once the economy returns to full employment. (c) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC. (d) Discuss whether the investment programme will make the people of Quentara better off.
items.answer: (a) 5 percentage points (b) Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. (c) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. (d) Outward shift of the PPC in future, more consumer goods later, jobs now (idle resources used: no opportunity cost in a recession) vs lower consumption at full employment, risk of poor projects, debt; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 9 − 4 [1] (b) Credit: Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. [2] (c) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2] (d) Credit: Outward shift of the PPC in future, more consumer goods later, jobs now (idle resources used: no opportunity cost in a recession) vs lower consumption at full employment, risk of poor projects, debt; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Extract: Productivity growth in Fendaria has been only 0.8% a year. The government plans to privatise the state railway, cut corporation tax, and raise spending on education to 3% of GDP. It hopes productivity growth will rise to 2.2%. Critics argue that privatisation will lead to higher fares and that tax cuts mainly benefit the rich. (a) Classify the three policies as market-based or interventionist. (b) Calculate the difference in output per worker after 10 years at the two productivity growth rates (start = 100). (c) Explain how higher education spending could increase LRAS. (d) Explain why privatisation might raise fares.
items.answer: (a) Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. (b) 108.3 vs 124.3 (c) Human capital raises productivity and potential output. (d) A private monopoly seeks profit and may raise prices or cut services unless regulated.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. [2] (b) Credit: 108.3 vs 124.3 [2] (c) Credit: Human capital raises productivity and potential output. [2] (d) Credit: A private monopoly seeks profit and may raise prices or cut services unless regulated. [2]

items.stem: A policy institute in Dhaka has published a report on this issue for the government of Calvania. Explain why prices in agricultural markets tend to be unstable.
items.answer: Supply shocks (weather, disease), inelastic supply and demand, time lags, cobweb behaviour, world market speculation; diagram.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Supply shocks (weather, disease), inelastic supply and demand, time lags, cobweb behaviour, world market speculation; diagram. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: The market for the baht is described by Qd = 850 − 5P and Qs = 500 + 2P, where P is the price of one baht in US cents and Q is millions of baht traded a day. (a) Calculate the equilibrium exchange rate and quantity. (b) Foreign demand for Nordavia’s exports rises, increasing demand for the baht by 14 million a day at every exchange rate. Calculate the new equilibrium exchange rate and quantity.
items.answer: (a) 7P = 350: P = 50 US cents, Q = 600 million. (b) New Qd = 864 − 5P: P = 52 US cents, Q = 604 million; the baht appreciates by 4%.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) new rate [1]; quantity [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The market for coffee in Cairo is described by Qd = 74 − 2P and Qs = 26 + 2P (Q in thousands per month, P in dollars). The city council is considering a tax on coffee, which some councillors say would “simply transfer money from consumers to the council”. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Discuss whether the councillors are right that the tax is “simply a transfer”.
items.answer: (a) $12, 50 (b) Not only a transfer: deadweight loss from fewer trades; size depends on elasticities; revenue may fund beneficial spending; externalities could make it welfare-improving; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $12, 50 [2] (b) Credit: Not only a transfer: deadweight loss from fewer trades; size depends on elasticities; revenue may fund beneficial spending; externalities could make it welfare-improving; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Identify the conflict in each case and explain it. (i) Fast growth in Istrana increases air pollution in Santiago. (ii) The central bank of Istrana raises interest rates to cut inflation, and unemployment rises.
items.answer: (i) Economic growth vs environmental sustainability (ii) Low inflation vs low unemployment
items.markingKey: (i) Economic growth vs environmental sustainability – more output creates more negative externalities. [2] (ii) Low inflation vs low unemployment – reducing AD lowers inflation but also output and jobs. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Which situation has a zero opportunity cost?
options: Buying a good that is on sale at half price
Receiving a good that the government provides free of charge
Using savings rather than borrowing to buy a good
Using a resource that has no alternative use
items.answer: Using a resource that has no alternative use
items.markingKey: If there is no alternative use, nothing is forgone.

items.stem: An appreciation of a country’s currency is likely to
options: shift AD to the left by reducing net exports
items.answer: shift AD to the left by reducing net exports
items.markingKey: Exports dearer, imports cheaper.

items.stem: Teachers in Zentara received a 4% pay rise while the CPI rose by 6%. Explain what happened to their living standards.
items.answer: Real pay fell by about 2%, so they can buy less than before.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: real fall ≈ 2%; 1 mark: purchasing power [2]

items.stem: Sugary fizzy drinks sold to teenagers in Kathmandu. How is this good best classified?
items.answer: Demerit good
items.markingKey: Demerit good: the harm to health is underestimated by consumers.

items.stem: During a class discussion Noah said: ‘Jovania has an absolute advantage in producing both goods, so it cannot gain from trading with Dravonia.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: Gains from trade depend on comparative, not absolute, advantage; as long as opportunity costs differ, both countries can gain by specialising.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Gains from trade depend on comparative, not absolute, advantage; as long as opportunity costs differ, both countries can gain by specialising. [2]

items.stem: In Rovania, the domestic demand for bicycles is Qd = 151 − 5P and domestic supply is Qs = 5 + 2P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units a year. Rovania can import any quantity at the world price of $12. The government imposes a tariff of $6 per unit. Calculate the quantity imported after the tariff.
items.answer: 20 thousand units
items.markingKey: At $18: Qd = 61, Qs = 41; imports = 20 thousand.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is an example of market failure? (b) Which is the main reason a government might provide a good itself?
items.answer: (a) The under-provision of public goods (b) The market would not provide it because of the free rider problem
items.markingKey: (a) Missing markets, externalities, information failure, merit/demerit goods. (b) Public goods.

items.stem: Why might supply-side policies improve the current account?
options: They make domestic firms more competitive internationally
items.answer: They make domestic firms more competitive internationally
items.markingKey: Lower costs, better quality.

items.stem: Many workers from Valdoria work abroad and send income home, while foreign firms in Valdoria send profits overseas. Explain how this affects the difference between Valdoria’s GDP and GNI.
items.answer: Income earned abroad by residents adds to GNI; profits paid to foreign owners are subtracted. GNI exceeds GDP if inflows are larger than outflows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflows add; 1 mark: outflows subtract [2]

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of healthcare and education that Westaria can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; healthcare: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; education: 350, 325, 275, 150, 0. Westaria is currently producing 10 units of healthcare and 375 units of education. Which describes this position?
options: On the PPC: the economy is experiencing economic growth
Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.answer: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.markingKey: At 10 units of healthcare the maximum of education is 325; 375 is more than this.

items.stem: Coffee growers in Kestria receive a higher world price after poor harvests elsewhere. Explain the effect on their producer surplus.
items.answer: They receive a higher price for every bag sold above the minimum they would accept, so producer surplus rises (if their own output is unaffected).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher price; 1 mark: larger area above supply [2]

items.stem: In Valdoria, national income is $500 billion. Households save 10%, pay 25% in tax and spend 10% on imports. Calculate spending on domestically produced goods and services.
items.answer: $275 billion

items.stem: The government of Ostrelia faces high unemployment caused by a fall in AD. Explain which type of policy would act most quickly.
items.answer: Demand-side policy: monetary policy (interest rate cuts) can be changed quickly; fiscal stimulus raises AD directly; supply-side policies take years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: demand-side; 1 mark: speed reasoning [2]

items.stem: To reduce a current account deficit of $10bn, the government of Sundara cuts its spending by $8bn. The multiplier is 2.5 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.25. Calculate the fall in national income.
items.answer: $20bn

items.stem: Mei makes the following statement: ‘Consumer sovereignty means that consumers set the prices of goods.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: It means consumers’ spending decisions determine what is produced; prices are set by the interaction of demand and supply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It means consumers’ spending decisions determine what is produced; prices are set by the interaction of demand and supply. [2]

items.stem: When the price of tomatoes (per box) rose from $40 to $44, the quantity supplied rose from 200 to 210 units a month. (a) Calculate the PES and state whether supply is elastic or inelastic. (b) Suggest two reasons why supply of tomatoes (per box) might have this elasticity.
items.answer: (a) PES = 0.5: price inelastic. (b) Long production time, no spare capacity, few stocks, immobile factors.
items.markingKey: (a) 5/10 = 0.5 [2]; interpretation [1] (b) two consistent reasons [2] [5]

items.stem: The government imposes an indirect tax on paper. What is the effect on the supply curve of paper?
options: Shift of the supply curve to the right
Shift of the supply curve to the left
items.answer: Shift of the supply curve to the left
items.markingKey: Shift of the supply curve to the left: the tax raises costs per unit.

items.stem: Amara wrote in a homework answer: ‘Equity means that everyone should have exactly the same income.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: Equity means fairness; equality means the same shares. A fair distribution may still be unequal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Equity means fairness; equality means the same shares. A fair distribution may still be unequal. [2]

items.stem: Silverline changes the price of its sun hats from $4 to $4.20. Weekly sales change from 1,200 to 1,140. Calculate the change in total revenue.
In a revision note Ravi wrote: ‘The rationing function of price means the government decides who gets scarce goods.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: In the price mechanism, rationing happens through price: goods go to those willing and able to pay; government rationing is an alternative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – In the price mechanism, rationing happens through price: goods go to those willing and able to pay; government rationing is an alternative. [2]

items.stem: A government bond in Lunaria pays a fixed $60 a year. After central bank purchases (quantitative easing), its market price rises from $800 to $880. (a) Calculate the yield before and after. (b) Explain how lower bond yields can lead to higher aggregate demand.
items.answer: (a) 7.5% → 6.82% (b) Lower yields reduce long-term borrowing costs (mortgages, corporate loans), encourage investment and consumption, raise asset prices and wealth, and may weaken the currency, raising net exports.
items.markingKey: (a) both yields [2] (b) borrowing costs [1]; spending/wealth [1] [4]

items.stem: In Loristan, 500 thousand people are unemployed. Each could produce output worth $20,000 a year. Each receives $6,000 in benefits and would pay $5,000 in tax if employed. (a) Calculate the output lost each year and the annual cost to the government budget. (b) Explain why the output lost is a better measure of the cost to society than the benefits paid.
items.answer: (a) Output lost $10bn; budget cost $5.5bn (benefits + lost tax). (b) Benefits are transfers from taxpayers to the unemployed and do not use up resources; lost output is the real opportunity cost to society.
items.markingKey: (a) lost output [1]; budget cost [1] (b) transfers vs real resources [2] [4]

items.stem: Extract: After a deep recession, the budget deficit in Zentara rose from 2% to 7% of GDP and national debt from 60% to 85% of GDP. Part of the rise was caused by automatic stabilisers; the rest by a discretionary programme of infrastructure spending and a temporary cut in VAT. The opposition calls for immediate spending cuts. (a) Calculate the increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio in percentage points. (b) Explain how automatic stabilisers increased the deficit. (c) Explain how the VAT cut and infrastructure spending were intended to affect AD.
items.answer: (a) 25 percentage points (b) Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending. (c) Higher disposable income/consumption and higher G raise AD, output and employment.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 25 percentage points [1] (b) Credit: Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending. [2] (c) Credit: Higher disposable income/consumption and higher G raise AD, output and employment. [3]

items.stem: The market for the won is described by Qd = 420 − 3P and Qs = 220 + 2P, where P is the price of one won in US cents and Q is millions of won traded a day. (a) Calculate the equilibrium exchange rate and quantity. (b) Foreign demand for Marvona’s exports rises, increasing demand for the won by 20 million a day at every exchange rate. Calculate the new equilibrium exchange rate and the percentage change in the value of the won. (c) Explain one effect of this change on Marvona’s economy.
items.answer: (a) 5P = 200: P = 40 US cents, Q = 300 million. (b) New Qd = 440 − 3P: P = 44 US cents, Q = 308 million; the won appreciates by 10%. (c) Exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so the current account may worsen and inflation fall.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) new rate [1]; % change [1] (c) [2] [6]

items.stem: Extract: In Nordavia the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 12 to 15 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 600 million to 540 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Explain how the government could use marginal analysis to decide the size of the tax. (c) Discuss whether the effects of the tax are likely to be greater in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 10% (b) Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). (c) In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) (600 − 540)/600 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). [2] (c) Credit: In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Extract: Annual growth of real GDP in Loristan over five years was 4.5%, 2%, −1%, −0.3% and 1.5%. The output gap is now estimated at −4% of potential GDP. The government plans to raise spending on infrastructure and training. Environmental groups warn that a return to rapid growth will increase pollution. (a) Identify the phases of the economic cycle shown by the data. (b) Explain what the output gap of −4% means. (c) Explain how infrastructure and training spending could lead to both actual and potential growth. (d) Explain one cost of economic growth mentioned in the extract.
items.answer: (a) Boom/slowdown (years 1–2), recession (years 3–4), recovery (year 5). (b) Actual output is below potential: spare capacity, unemployment, low inflationary pressure. (c) Raises AD now (using spare capacity) and LRAS later (productivity). (d) Pollution: negative externality, health costs, not measured in GDP.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Boom/slowdown (years 1–2), recession (years 3–4), recovery (year 5). [2] (b) Credit: Actual output is below potential: spare capacity, unemployment, low inflationary pressure. [2] (c) Credit: Raises AD now (using spare capacity) and LRAS later (productivity). [3] (d) Credit: Pollution: negative externality, health costs, not measured in GDP. [2]

items.stem: Dravonia’s large surplus causes its currency to appreciate and trading partners to complain. Which consequence of a current account imbalance is described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Pressure for appreciation and international tension: surpluses mean deficits elsewhere and demand for the currency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Pressure for appreciation and international tension; 1 mark: explanation – surpluses mean deficits elsewhere and demand for the currency. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Quarry Bay Ltd makes bottled water in Kathmandu. Five years ago it employed 30 craft workers who each made complete products. It now employs 18 workers on a production line, each doing one task, with new machinery. Monthly output has risen from 500 to 900 units. The founder, Lucas, says the change was a risk because she borrowed heavily to buy the machines. (a) Identify two factors of production mentioned in the extract and their rewards. (b) Explain the risk taken by the founder as an entrepreneur. (c) Discuss whether the workers have benefited from the change.
items.answer: (a) Labour (workers) → wages; capital (machinery) → interest; enterprise (the founder) → profit. (b) Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital. (c) Fewer jobs (some made redundant), repetitive tasks, deskilling vs possibly higher wages from higher productivity, safer work, job security if the firm is more competitive; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each factor with reward [2] (b) Credit: Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital. [2] (c) Credit: Fewer jobs (some made redundant), repetitive tasks, deskilling vs possibly higher wages from higher productivity, safer work, job security if the firm is more competitive; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Identify the unintended consequence in each case and explain why it arose. (i) A ban on single-use plastic bags in Toronto increased the use of thicker bags made from more plastic. (ii) A subsidy to farmers in Merania produced large surpluses that had to be stored.
items.answer: (i) Substitution into other harmful goods (ii) Over-production and waste
items.markingKey: (i) Substitution into other harmful goods – consumers switched to alternatives with their own problems. [2] (ii) Over-production and waste – the subsidy encouraged output beyond what consumers want. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Westaria has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($150 million), a rail link to Dhaka ($300 million) and a programme of school building ($350 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (c) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem. (d) Discuss how the government should decide which project to fund.
items.answer: (a) $400 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (c) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost. (d) Compare benefits and opportunity costs; consider who gains (for whom), long-run effects on growth, equity and public opinion; data may be uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 150 + 300 + 350 = 800; |800 − 1200| = 400 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (c) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2] (d) 2 marks: analysis of criteria; 2 marks: evaluation and conclusion [4]

items.stem: Hana, an economics student in Istanbul, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. With the help of AD/AS diagrams, explain how an increase in aggregate demand affects real output and the price level.
items.answer: Depends on spare capacity: Keynesian AS with flat, rising and vertical sections; classical vertical LRAS; diagrams.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Depends on spare capacity: Keynesian AS with flat, rising and vertical sections; classical vertical LRAS; diagrams. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: The CPI in Merania was 100 two years ago, 104 last year and 111 this year. Energy prices rose sharply after a global supply shock, and the central bank warns of a wage–price spiral. Average wages rose by 4% this year. Pensioners and savers complain that their living standards are falling. (a) Calculate the approximate change in real wages this year. (b) Explain why pensioners and savers lose from inflation. (c) Discuss whether a wage–price spiral is likely to develop.
items.answer: (a) −2.7% (b) Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings. (c) Depends on expectations, union power, labour market tightness, central bank credibility and whether the energy shock is temporary; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 − 6.7 [1] (b) Credit: Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings. [3] (c) Credit: Depends on expectations, union power, labour market tightness, central bank credibility and whether the energy shock is temporary; judgement. [4]

items.stem: In Zentara, 50% of children receive a flu vaccination when parents must pay $25. When the vaccination was made free in a trial region, take-up rose to 90%. The national child population is 200,000. (a) Calculate the cost to the government of free vaccinations nationally at the trial take-up rate, in millions of dollars. (b) Using the concept of a merit good, explain why take-up was low when parents paid. (c) Explain one reason why the policy may be worth its cost.
items.answer: (a) $4.5 million (b) Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure) and ignore benefits to others, so demand is below the social optimum. (c) External benefits: fewer infections in the wider population, lower healthcare costs and fewer days lost from work.
items.markingKey: (a) 200,000 × 90% × $25 = $4.5m [2] (b) information failure/under-consumption [1] (c) external benefits/savings [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Tarvia and Sundara are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Tarvia can produce 6 tonnes of rice or 3 metres of cloth a week; one worker in Sundara can produce 12 tonnes of rice or 8 metres of cloth. Over the last five years Tarvia’s export price index has moved to 118 and its import price index to 100 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Tarvia fear job losses in its cloth industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of 1 unit of rice in each country. (b) Calculate Tarvia’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (c) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) Tarvia: 0.5 metres of cloth; Sundara: 0.67 metres of cloth. (b) 118/100 × 100 = 118; improved (favourable). (c) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Tarvia: 0.5 metres of cloth; Sundara: 0.67 metres of cloth. [2] (b) Credit: 118/100 × 100 = 118; improved (favourable). [2] (c) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: A tariff on imported smartphones in Marvona raises consumers’ spending on smartphones by $200m a year and is estimated to save 2,400 jobs in domestic factories. The average wage in the industry is $22,000 a year. (a) Calculate the cost to consumers of each job saved and compare it with the average wage. (b) Explain two other costs of the tariff not included in this figure. (c) Discuss whether saving these jobs justifies the tariff.
items.answer: (a) $83,333, 3.8 times the average wage. (b) Retaliation against Marvona’s exports; higher costs for firms using smartphones; reduced competition and efficiency; deadweight loss. (c) Jobs are concentrated in particular regions and unemployment has social costs; but the cost per job is high, other jobs may be lost, and retraining or regional policy may be cheaper; temporary protection may be justified if the industry can become competitive; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) calculation [1]; comparison [1] (b) two costs [2] (c) evaluation [3] [7]

items.stem: Which is a disadvantage of a market economy?
options: Firms have no incentive to be efficient
Prices do not respond to demand
Public goods are likely not to be provided
items.answer: Public goods are likely not to be provided
items.markingKey: Market failure: public goods, externalities, inequality.

items.stem: Which is a reason for an individual’s demand to be shown by a demand schedule?
options: It lists the quantities the consumer would buy at different prices in a given time period
It shows the costs of production
It lists the prices set by firms
It shows how much the consumer earns
items.answer: It lists the quantities the consumer would buy at different prices in a given time period
items.markingKey: Demand schedule: table of P and Qd.

items.stem: Redwood Corp uses its factory to make car tyres instead of bottled water. Explain the opportunity cost to Redwood Corp.
items.answer: The profit (or output) from making bottled water, the next best use of the factory, is given up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forgone output/profit of electric scooters; 1 mark: next best use of the resources [3]

items.stem: A neighbourhood in Muscat has 500 households. Each values a new set of street lights at $20. The lights would cost $8,000 to install. Calculate the total value of the lights to the households.
Teachers in Nordavia received a 4% pay rise while the CPI rose by 6%. Explain what happened to their living standards.
items.answer: Real pay fell by about 2%, so they can buy less than before.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: real fall ≈ 2%; 1 mark: purchasing power [3]

items.stem: Estimates for Pelora: the price elasticity of demand for exports is −0.2 in the short run and −1 in the long run; for imports it is −0.2 in the short run and −0.7 in the long run. Imports make up 20% of the consumer price index. The currency depreciates by 20%. What is the likely effect on the current account?
options: It worsens in both the short run and the long run
It worsens in the short run and improves in the long run
It improves in both the short run and the long run
It improves in the short run and worsens in the long run
items.answer: It worsens in the short run and improves in the long run
items.markingKey: Short run sum 0.4 < 1 (worsens); long run sum 1.7 > 1 (Marshall–Lerner met, improves): J-curve.

items.stem: Why might supply-side policies not be suitable for correcting a current account deficit quickly?
options: They take a long time to have an effect
items.answer: They take a long time to have an effect
items.markingKey: Long time lags.

items.stem: How can economic growth improve government finances?
options: Tax revenues rise and spending on benefits falls
items.answer: Tax revenues rise and spending on benefits falls
items.markingKey: Fiscal dividend.

items.stem: Diego makes the following statement: ‘GDP at basic prices is GDP at market prices plus indirect taxes.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Basic prices = market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Basic prices = market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies. [3]

items.stem: In the market for cement, Qd = 200 − 10P and Qs = 40 + 6P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government introduces a maximum price of $7. Calculate the shortage that results.
items.answer: 48 thousand units
items.markingKey: Qd = 130, Qs = 82 at $7; difference 48.

items.stem: During a recession the budget deficit of Merania rose from 2% to 6% of GDP although tax rates and benefit rules were unchanged. Explain why.
items.answer: Automatic stabilisers: falling incomes and spending cut tax revenue and rising unemployment raised benefit spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: revenue fell; 1 mark: spending rose [3]

items.stem: Kestria finances its large current account deficit by borrowing heavily from abroad. Which consequence of a current account imbalance is described?
items.answer: Rising foreign debt
items.markingKey: Rising foreign debt: future interest payments increase primary income debits.

items.stem: Sofia wrote in a homework answer: ‘Quantitative easing means the government spends more on public services.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: QE is a monetary policy: the central bank buys financial assets to increase the money supply; it is not government spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – QE is a monetary policy: the central bank buys financial assets to increase the money supply; it is not government spending. [3]

items.stem: Average income in Jovania rose from $25,000 to $27,000, and monthly sales of electric scooters changed from 2,000 to 1920 units. Calculate the income elasticity of demand.
Kenji makes the following statement: ‘Free trade benefits every worker in Halvoria.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers. [3]

items.stem: Exports from Gorvania fall because of a global recession. What is the likely effect on national income, other things equal? Explain your answer.
items.answer: National income falls: exports are an injection.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: National income falls; 1 mark: explanation – exports are an injection. [3]

items.stem: Quarry Bay Ltd produces 1000 units a week in one factory. Overtime can raise output by up to 10% within a month. A new production line, taking 6 months to install, would raise capacity by 60%. Calculate the maximum weekly output possible in the short run.
items.answer: 1100 units

items.stem: Halvoria wants to develop a domestic car tyres industry. Explain why it might use protection, and what conditions would make this successful.
items.answer: Infant industry: temporary protection while firms grow and gain economies of scale. It works only if protection is time-limited, firms invest and become efficient, and there is a real potential comparative advantage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: infant industry; 1 mark: condition (temporary/potential CA/investment) [3]

items.stem: Hana receives a state pension each month. Is this an example of income or wealth?
items.answer: Income
items.markingKey: Income: a transfer payment received over time.

items.stem: The government of Valdoria offers start-up loans to young entrepreneurs. Explain why it might do this.
items.answer: To encourage new firms, jobs, innovation and competition; entrepreneurs often lack access to finance because banks see them as risky.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefits of enterprise; 1 mark: finance barrier [2]

items.stem: A major earthquake destroys many factories and roads in Westaria. How would this be shown on the country’s PPC? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Inward shift of the PPC: capital is destroyed, reducing productive capacity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Inward shift of the PPC; 1 mark: explanation – capital is destroyed, reducing productive capacity. [2]

items.stem: No private firm in Merania will build a flood barrier because residents who do not pay would still be protected. Which type of market failure is illustrated? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Public good (free rider problem): non-excludable; free riders mean no revenue so the market is missing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Public good (free rider problem); 1 mark: explanation – non-excludable; free riders mean no revenue so the market is missing. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Westaria is growing at 4% a year and unemployment is only 4.5%. However, inflation has risen to 5.5% (target 2%) and the current account deficit is 4.5% of GDP. The finance minister wants to keep growth high; the central bank wants to raise interest rates. (a) Explain how rapid growth may have caused the inflation and the current account deficit. (b) Explain the conflict between the finance minister’s and the central bank’s aims.
items.answer: (a) Demand above capacity → demand-pull inflation; higher incomes → more imports. (b) Higher interest rates reduce inflation and imports but slow growth and raise unemployment.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Demand above capacity → demand-pull inflation; higher incomes → more imports. [4] (b) Credit: Higher interest rates reduce inflation and imports but slow growth and raise unemployment. [2]

items.stem: The market for bus journeys in Lunaria is described by Qd = 300 − 4P and Qs = 75 + 5P, where Q is in thousands of units a week and P in dollars. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Calculate the shortage if the price were $15. (c) Explain how the market would return to equilibrium.
items.answer: (a) P = $25, Q = 200 thousand. (b) At $15: Qd = 240, Qs = 150: excess demand of 90 thousand. (c) Price rises; Qd contracts and Qs extends until equal.
items.markingKey: (a) solve 300 − 4P = 75 + 5P [1]; P and Q [1] (b) Qd and Qs at $15 [1]; difference [1] (c) adjustment process [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: The market for electric scooters in Bogotá is described by Qd = 170 − 10P and Qs = 2 + 4P (Q in thousands per month, P in dollars). The city council is considering a tax on electric scooters, which some councillors say would “simply transfer money from consumers to the council”. (a) Calculate consumer surplus at equilibrium. (b) Calculate producer surplus at equilibrium. (c) Discuss whether the councillors are right that the tax is “simply a transfer”.
items.answer: (a) $125,000 (b) $312,000 (c) Not only a transfer: deadweight loss from fewer trades; size depends on elasticities; revenue may fund beneficial spending; externalities could make it welfare-improving; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) ½ × (17 − 12) × 50 [2] (b) Credit: $312,000 [2] (c) Credit: Not only a transfer: deadweight loss from fewer trades; size depends on elasticities; revenue may fund beneficial spending; externalities could make it welfare-improving; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Extract: Productivity growth in Calvania has been only 1.0% a year. The government plans to privatise the state railway, cut corporation tax, and raise spending on education to 5% of GDP. It hopes productivity growth will rise to 2.5%. Critics argue that privatisation will lead to higher fares and that tax cuts mainly benefit the rich. (a) Classify the three policies as market-based or interventionist. (b) Explain how higher education spending could increase LRAS. (c) Discuss whether these supply-side policies are likely to raise productivity growth.
items.answer: (a) Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. (b) Human capital raises productivity and potential output. (c) Incentives, investment and skills vs time lags, uncertainty, private monopoly, inequality, funding; depends on implementation; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. [2] (b) Credit: Human capital raises productivity and potential output. [2] (c) Credit: Incentives, investment and skills vs time lags, uncertainty, private monopoly, inequality, funding; depends on implementation; judgement. [5]

items.stem: In Esteria, aggregate demand was $920bn. Over the year consumption changed by +20bn, investment by −15bn, exports by −20bn and imports by +10bn; government spending was unchanged. (a) Calculate the new AD and the percentage change. (b) State and explain the direction of the shift in the AD curve and suggest one possible cause of the change in investment.
items.answer: (a) $895bn; −2.7%. (b) AD shifts left; investment change could reflect a change in interest rates or business confidence.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) direction [1]; cause [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The unemployment rate in Istrana rose from 6% to 10.5% over two years, while youth unemployment rose from 10% to 19%. Job losses have been concentrated in manufacturing as firms automate, but retail and construction also cut jobs as consumer spending fell. Vacancies for software engineers remain unfilled. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the unemployment rate. (b) Identify two types of unemployment indicated by the extract and explain your choice. (c) Explain two consequences of high youth unemployment.
items.answer: (a) 75% (b) Structural (automation, unfilled skilled vacancies: mismatch); cyclical (fall in consumer spending). (c) Lost skills/hysteresis, lower lifetime earnings, social problems, emigration, lost output.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 75% [2] (b) Credit: Structural (automation, unfilled skilled vacancies: mismatch); cyclical (fall in consumer spending). [4] (c) Credit: Lost skills/hysteresis, lower lifetime earnings, social problems, emigration, lost output. [2]

items.stem: Demand for fresh fish increases so that, at the original price, buyers want 30% more. The PES is 2 and the PED is −1. (a) Using %ΔP = (shift in demand %) ÷ (PES − PED), calculate the percentage change in price and in quantity. (b) Explain why the effect on price would be different if supply were much more elastic.
items.answer: (a) %ΔP ≈ 10%; %ΔQ ≈ 20%. (b) With more elastic supply, output expands more easily, so more of the adjustment is in quantity and the price rises less.
items.markingKey: (a) 30/3 = 10 [1]; 2 × 10 = 20 [1] (b) elastic supply → smaller price rise [2] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Lunaria was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 2.0% to 6.5%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.28 to 0.42, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the Gini coefficient. (b) Explain why growth may have increased after the reforms. (c) Discuss whether the move to a market economy has been beneficial for the people of Lunaria.
items.answer: (a) 50% (b) Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. (c) Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) (0.42 − 0.28)/0.28 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. [3] (c) Credit: Growth, choice, efficiency vs inequality, insecurity, possible unemployment; state still corrects market failures; depends on who gains and on views of equity; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Nadia, an economics student in Jakarta, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. With the help of diagrams, explain the difference between a movement along and a shift of a demand curve.
items.answer: Own price → extension/contraction; conditions of demand (income, related goods, tastes, population, expectations) → shift; diagrams showing both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Own price → extension/contraction; conditions of demand (income, related goods, tastes, population, expectations) → shift; diagrams showing both. items.stem: A policy institute in Dubai has published a report on this issue for the government of Umbria Nova. Explain the three basic economic questions that every economy has to answer.
items.answer: What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning). items.stem: In Dravonia, 45% of children receive a flu vaccination when parents must pay $25. When the vaccination was made free in a trial region, take-up rose to 85%. The national child population is 400,000. (a) Calculate the cost to the government of free vaccinations nationally at the trial take-up rate, in millions of dollars. (b) Using the concept of a merit good, explain why take-up was low when parents paid. (c) Explain one reason why the policy may be worth its cost.
items.answer: (a) $8.5 million (b) Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure) and ignore benefits to others, so demand is below the social optimum. (c) External benefits: fewer infections in the wider population, lower healthcare costs and fewer days lost from work.
items.markingKey: (a) 400,000 × 85% × $25 = $8.5m [2] (b) information failure/under-consumption [1] (c) external benefits/savings [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The CPI in Tarvia was 100 two years ago, 104 last year and 111 this year. Energy prices rose sharply after a global supply shock, and the central bank warns of a wage–price spiral. Average wages rose by 3% this year. Pensioners and savers complain that their living standards are falling. (a) Calculate the inflation rate in each of the two years. (b) Discuss whether a wage–price spiral is likely to develop.
items.answer: (a) +4%, +6.7% (b) Depends on expectations, union power, labour market tightness, central bank credibility and whether the energy shock is temporary; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: +4%, +6.7% [2] (b) Credit: Depends on expectations, union power, labour market tightness, central bank credibility and whether the energy shock is temporary; judgement. [4]

items.stem: In the foreign exchange market for the rand, demand is Qd = 720 − 3P and supply is Qs = 360 + 6P, where P is the price of one rand in US cents and Q is millions of rand a day. The central bank of Fendaria fixes the exchange rate at 50 US cents per rand. (a) Calculate the free-market equilibrium exchange rate. (b) Calculate the excess supply at the fixed rate. (c) Calculate the US dollars the central bank must spend each day to maintain the rate. (d) Explain two ways the central bank could avoid running down its reserves.
items.answer: (a) Free-market rate: Qd = 720 − 3P = Qs = 360 + 6P gives P = 40 US cents, Q = 600 million. (b) At 50 cents: Qd = 570, Qs = 660; excess supply = 90 million rand a day. (c) It must buy 90 million rand at $0.5 each = $45 million a day. (d) Raise interest rates to attract capital inflows (raising demand for the rand); use contractionary policies or controls to reduce imports (lowering supply); or devalue to the market rate.

items.stem: Why is demand for petrol more price elastic in the long run than in the short run?
options: Consumers have more time to find substitutes such as electric cars or public transport
Incomes always rise in the long run
Petrol prices fall in the long run
Petrol becomes a necessity over time
items.answer: Consumers have more time to find substitutes such as electric cars or public transport
items.markingKey: Time allows adjustment.

items.stem: Why are public goods usually provided by the government?
options: Private firms cannot charge consumers because non-payers cannot be excluded
They are too cheap to produce privately
items.answer: Private firms cannot charge consumers because non-payers cannot be excluded
items.markingKey: Missing market due to free riding.

items.stem: A student, Jonas, claims: ‘VAT is a direct tax because consumers pay it directly when they buy goods.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: VAT is an indirect tax: it is levied on spending and collected by sellers, not levied on income or wealth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – VAT is an indirect tax: it is levied on spending and collected by sellers, not levied on income or wealth. [2]

items.stem: Tarvia spends $8bn on a training programme for 250,000 workers. Each trained worker’s output rises by $5,000 a year for 10 years. Calculate the total extra output over the period (ignoring discounting).
The government of Quentara has a fixed budget but faces demands for more hospitals, schools and roads. Explain how this illustrates the basic economic problem.
items.answer: The government’s resources (its budget) are limited, while the demands on them are effectively unlimited, so it must choose which projects to fund and which to go without.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limited budget/resources; 1 mark: unlimited demands so choices must be made [2]

items.stem: Consumers in Quentara buy cars made abroad. Is this an injection into or a leakage from the circular flow?
options: Neither: a transfer within the flow
items.answer: Leakage (withdrawal)
items.markingKey: Leakage (withdrawal): imports send spending out of the domestic flow.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is a negative externality? (b) Which is an example of market failure?
items.answer: (a) A cost imposed on a third party that is not reflected in the market price (b) The under-provision of public goods
items.markingKey: (a) External cost; e.g. pollution. (b) Missing markets, externalities, information failure, merit/demerit goods.

items.stem: What is a risk for a country that specialises heavily in one export?
options: Its terms of trade must improve
Its income becomes vulnerable to a fall in world demand or price for that good
It cannot benefit from comparative advantage
items.answer: Its income becomes vulnerable to a fall in world demand or price for that good
items.markingKey: Over-specialisation increases exposure to shocks.

items.stem: A student, Jonas, claims: ‘Regulation has no costs for the government because firms simply obey the rules.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Regulations must be monitored and enforced, which uses resources; firms may evade them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Regulations must be monitored and enforced, which uses resources; firms may evade them. [2]

items.stem: A new irrigation technology raises crop yields in Sundara but has no effect on manufacturing. How would this be shown on the country’s PPC?
options: Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis
items.answer: Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis
items.markingKey: Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis: only the maximum output of food rises.

items.stem: Diego wrote in a homework answer: ‘Protection always saves jobs in Halvoria overall.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs. [2]

items.stem: In Esteria, nominal GDP rose from $500 billion in the base year to $540 billion a year later. The GDP deflator rose from 100 to 112. Calculate real GDP in the second year at base-year prices.
items.answer: $482.1 billion

items.stem: Most mortgages in Jovania have variable interest rates. Explain why this makes monetary policy more powerful.
items.answer: A change in the policy rate quickly changes mortgage payments and disposable income, so consumption responds faster and more strongly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: payments change quickly; 1 mark: consumption response [2]

items.stem: Planners in Istrana set the price of flats below the market level. At this price 480 thousand households want to buy flats each year, but the plan provides only 300 thousand. Calculate the shortage as a percentage of the quantity supplied.
The price of tickets for a football final in Mexico City doubles but the number of seats stays the same. Explain what this shows about PES.
items.answer: Supply is perfectly inelastic (PES = 0): the stadium has a fixed capacity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: PES = 0; 1 mark: fixed capacity [2]

items.stem: Dravonia: Year: 1, 2, 3, 4; Real GDP ($ billion): 400, 408, 424.3, 445.5. (a) Calculate the growth rate in each of Years 2 to 4 and over the whole period. (b) Comment on the performance of the economy.
items.answer: (a) +2%, +4%, +5%; overall +11.4%. (b) Positive growth throughout; growth was uneven, and per capita and distribution data would be needed to judge living standards.
items.markingKey: (a) three annual rates [2]; overall [1] (b) comment using data [1] [4]

items.stem: The supply of steel pipes is Qs = 0 + 5P and demand is Qd = 100 − 5P, with Q in thousands and P in dollars. The market is in equilibrium at P = $10. Calculate producer surplus.

Answer both parts. (a) Explain why economists might agree on positive statements but disagree on normative statements. (b) Explain why government policy decisions usually involve normative judgements.
items.answer: (a) Positive statements can be settled by evidence, but normative statements depend on value judgements (e.g. about fairness), which differ between people. (b) Policies create winners and losers; choosing between them requires judgements about what is fair or desirable, not only facts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: positive testable; 1 mark: normative depend on values [2] (b) 1 mark: trade-offs/winners and losers; 1 mark: value judgement required [2]

items.stem: The exchange rate between the won and the US dollar changes from $1 = 5 won to $1 = 4 won. By what percentage has the value of the won in US dollars changed?
Apex Ltd has bought new machines for its factory in Dubai. Explain why this is described as investment.
items.answer: It adds to the capital stock, raising future capacity to produce steel pipes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capital goods; 1 mark: future production [2]

items.stem: Consumer spending in Jovania surges after a large tax cut while the economy is at full capacity. Which type of inflation is most likely? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Demand-pull inflation: AD rises faster than the economy can supply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Demand-pull inflation; 1 mark: explanation – AD rises faster than the economy can supply. [2]

items.stem: In Zentara, a worker on benefits earns an extra $100 a week. Income tax of 10% is paid on the extra earnings, and the means-tested benefit is withdrawn at 60 cents for each dollar of after-tax earnings. (a) Calculate the amount the worker keeps and the effective marginal tax rate. (b) Explain how this illustrates the poverty trap and suggest one policy to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) Keeps $36; effective marginal rate 64%. (b) High combined withdrawal of benefits and tax means little gain from working more, discouraging work; reduce the taper rate, raise tax-free allowance, or use in-work benefits.

items.stem: Extract: Selmaria’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 180, imports of goods 320, exports of services 95, imports of services 40, primary income balance −8, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain two possible causes of the deficit on trade in goods.
items.answer: (a) −$83bn; −6.9% of GDP. (b) Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$83bn; −6.9% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. [4]

items.stem: To reduce a current account deficit of $20bn, the government of Tarvia cuts its spending by $12bn. The multiplier is 2.5 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.3. GDP is $500bn. (a) Calculate the fall in national income and the fall in imports. (b) Calculate the new current account deficit, assuming exports are unchanged. (c) Calculate the cut in government spending needed to remove the deficit entirely by this method. (d) Comment on the cost of using this policy.
items.answer: (a) ΔY = 12 × 2.5 = −$30bn; ΔM = 0.3 × $30bn = −$9bn. (b) New deficit = $20bn − $9bn = $11bn. (c) Need ΔM = $20bn: ΔY = $20bn/0.3 = $66.7bn, so cut G = $66.7bn/2.5 = $26.7bn. (d) National income would fall by $66.7bn, about 13.3% of GDP, implying a large rise in unemployment; expenditure-switching or supply-side policies would be less costly.

items.stem: Extract: In Kestria, world oil prices rose by 50% this year. Inflation rose from 2.5% to 6.5% while real GDP growth slowed from 3% to 1%. At the same time, the government has announced a large programme of training and infrastructure investment, and consumer confidence has fallen. (a) Calculate the change in the inflation rate in percentage points. (b) Explain how the training and infrastructure programme could affect both AD and LRAS. (c) Discuss whether the government’s programme will reduce inflation in the long run.
items.answer: (a) 4 percentage points (b) G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run. (c) LRAS shift lowers price pressure, but AD boost now may add to inflation; time lags; size of programme vs oil shock; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 4 percentage points [1] (b) Credit: G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run. [3] (c) Credit: LRAS shift lowers price pressure, but AD boost now may add to inflation; time lags; size of programme vs oil shock; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Extract: Sundara is growing at 5% a year and unemployment is only 3.5%. However, inflation has risen to 7% (target 2%) and the current account deficit is 6% of GDP. The finance minister wants to keep growth high; the central bank wants to raise interest rates. (a) Explain how rapid growth may have caused the inflation and the current account deficit. (b) Discuss which policy mix would best achieve the government’s objectives.
items.answer: (a) Demand above capacity → demand-pull inflation; higher incomes → more imports. (b) Contractionary monetary policy to cut inflation; supply-side policies to raise capacity and competitiveness; fiscal restraint; time lags and trade-offs; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Demand above capacity → demand-pull inflation; higher incomes → more imports. [4] (b) Credit: Contractionary monetary policy to cut inflation; supply-side policies to raise capacity and competitiveness; fiscal restraint; time lags and trade-offs; judgement. [5]

items.stem: In Valdoria, the number of cattle slaughtered for beef rose from 400 thousand to 500 thousand a year after demand for beef increased. Each animal provides one hide used for leather. The price of leather was $25 per hide. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the supply of hides. (b) Explain, with reference to joint supply, the likely effect on the price of leather. (c) Explain why the size of the effect depends on the price elasticity of demand for leather.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) Leather is in joint supply with beef: supply of hides shifts right, so the price of leather falls and quantity rises. (c) If demand for leather is inelastic, a large fall in price is needed to sell the extra hides; if elastic, price falls only slightly.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) joint supply [1]; supply shifts right, price falls [1] (c) PED explanation [2] [5]

items.stem: The government of Fendaria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain the consequences of unemployment for individuals, firms and the economy.
items.answer: Income loss, skills, health; firms: lower demand but cheaper labour; economy: lost output, budget, inequality, social costs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Income loss, skills, health; firms: lower demand but cheaper labour; economy: lost output, budget, inequality, social costs. items.stem: The demand for rice in Lunaria is Qd = 200 − 5P. After a rise in the price of a substitute, demand becomes Qd = 250 − 5P. (a) Calculate the quantity demanded at $12 before and after the change. (b) State whether this is a shift or a movement along the demand curve and explain why. (c) Explain the cause using the conditions of demand.
items.answer: (a) 140 → 190 units. (b) A shift right: quantity demanded changes at every price, not because of the good’s own price. (c) The rise in the price of a substitute changes a condition of demand.
items.markingKey: (a) both values [2] (b) shift and direction [1]; reason [1] (c) cause explained [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: Research for the government of Gorvania estimates that the PED for petrol is −0.3, the YED for air travel is +1.8 and the XED between bus travel and the price of petrol is +0.8. The government plans a tax that would raise the price of petrol by 15%. Incomes are forecast to grow by 3% next year. (a) Calculate the expected percentage change in petrol consumption after the tax. (b) Explain why the PED for petrol is likely to be inelastic. (c) Calculate the expected change in demand for air travel and explain what the YED value shows. (d) Discuss whether the petrol tax will achieve both a large rise in tax revenue and a large fall in pollution.
items.answer: (a) −4.5% (b) Few close substitutes in the short run, necessity for commuting and business, habit. (c) +5.4%; luxury good, demand grows faster than income. (d) Inelastic demand → revenue rises but consumption falls little; conflict between objectives; long-run PED higher (electric cars, buses with XED > 0); estimates uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) −0.3 × 15 [1] (b) Credit: Few close substitutes in the short run, necessity for commuting and business, habit. [2] (c) Credit: +5.4%; luxury good, demand grows faster than income. [2] (d) Credit: Inelastic demand → revenue rises but consumption falls little; conflict between objectives; long-run PED higher (electric cars, buses with XED > 0); estimates uncertain; judgement. items.stem: Extract: The government of Merania has introduced a 30% tax on sugary drinks and used the revenue to fund free fruit in primary schools and a new public park in Accra. The share of adults who drink sugary drinks daily fell from 28% to 24%. Some critics argue that people should be free to choose what they consume. (a) Explain why the park is likely to be provided by the government rather than the market. (b) Discuss whether the government is right to interfere with consumers’ choices in this way.
items.answer: (a) It is (quasi-)public: non-excludable and largely non-rivalrous, so free riding means firms cannot charge. (b) Correcting information failure and external costs (healthcare) vs paternalism, regressive tax, possible substitution to other unhealthy goods; information campaigns as alternative; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: It is (quasi-)public: non-excludable and largely non-rivalrous, so free riding means firms cannot charge. [3] (b) Credit: Correcting information failure and external costs (healthcare) vs paternalism, regressive tax, possible substitution to other unhealthy goods; information campaigns as alternative; judgement. [5]

items.stem: Amara, an economics student in Doha, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. Explain how automatic stabilisers work and how they differ from discretionary fiscal policy.
items.answer: Progressive taxes and benefits change with the cycle; no decision lag; discretionary = deliberate changes; examples.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Progressive taxes and benefits change with the cycle; no decision lag; discretionary = deliberate changes; examples. items.stem: Samuel earns $30 an hour for overtime. The marginal income tax rate is cut from 40% to 30%. (a) Calculate the post-tax hourly reward before and after, and the percentage increase. (b) Explain why the tax cut may or may not increase the hours that Samuel chooses to work.
items.answer: (a) $18 → $21: +16.7%. (b) Substitution effect: leisure is now dearer, so more hours; income effect: the same income can be earned with fewer hours, so some may work less; the net effect is uncertain.
items.markingKey: (a) both [1]; % [1] (b) substitution vs income effect [2] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Quentara has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($350 million), a rail link to Dubai ($200 million) and a programme of school building ($150 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem. (b) Discuss how the government should decide which project to fund.
items.answer: (a) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost. (b) Compare benefits and opportunity costs; consider who gains (for whom), long-run effects on growth, equity and public opinion; data may be uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2] (b) 2 marks: analysis of criteria; 2 marks: evaluation and conclusion [4]

items.stem: Data for Tarvia: Item ($ billion): Investment, Saving, Government spending, Taxation, Exports, Imports; Value: 100, 110, 150, 160, 180, 170. (a) Calculate total injections and total leakages. (b) Explain what will happen to national income.
items.answer: (a) Injections $430bn; leakages $440bn. (b) National income will fall: more is withdrawn than added, so income falls until leakages equal injections.
items.markingKey: (a) both totals [2] (b) direction [1]; explanation [1] [4]
